title: Sampling choices

blocks.heading: Sampling choices
blocks.text:
Random, stratified and systematic sampling use different explicit selection procedures. Start with a relevant frame, justify size and selection, record non-response and avoid silently replacing a refusal with a friend. No sample guarantees perfect representativeness.

Applied example: A selection procedure can only choose members covered by its list. Missing a group from that frame can bias coverage even when selection from the list is fair.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Random sampling
blocks.text:
Random sampling selects by chance so each member of the defined research population has an equal chance of selection. Number a complete list and use a fair draw or random numbers without duplicates. Selecting whoever is nearest does not meet that rule.

Applied example: Distance from the researcher determines who is selected, so other households do not have an equal chance. A fair draw from a complete numbered list provides the required chance procedure.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Stratified sampling
blocks.text:
Stratified sampling divides a population into relevant groups and selects from each using an explicit method. For proportional selection, allocate sample places by each group’s share, then randomly select within groups. It preserves planned group coverage but cannot remove every frame or response bias.

Applied example: It deliberately allocates places to both groups in proportion to their population shares. A smaller group is therefore included by design, although non-response can still distort the final evidence.

blocks.heading: Systematic sampling
blocks.text:
Systematic sampling selects at a fixed interval from an ordered list after an appropriate starting point. For 60 households and 12 places, interval is five; a fair start among positions one to five can produce a reproducible selection. A repeating pattern in the list may bias it.

Applied example: A repeating list pattern can coincide with the selection interval. The sample may then overrepresent one type of unit even though a fixed rule was followed.

blocks.heading: Worked enquiry connection
blocks.text: Name and describe stratified sampling for this fictional task: 12 households from groups of 40 and 20. Stratified sampling: Allocate eight and four places proportionally, then fairly select distinct numbered households within each group. Record frame coverage and refusals rather than substitute convenient respondents.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Sampling calculations and frames
blocks.text: For a fictional list of 60 households and a sample of 12 (ITEM-6136-10.1-P01), 60 divided by 12 gives interval five; a fair starting position three gives 3,8,13,18,23,28,33,38,43,48,53,58. For fictional villages of 40 and 20 households (ITEM-6136-10.1-P02), the group proportions are 40/60 and 20/60: a 12-unit proportional allocation gives eight and four, followed by random selection within each. For a fictional list of 20 schools (ITEM-6136-10.1-P03), a fair draw of five distinct school numbers is random selection; the actual sample is the schools selected, not the drawing procedure. Record non-response and frame limitations.
